title: I like the music
goal: Say what you like, dislike and miss with a pattern that flips your instincts: the subject of the sentence is not you, but **the thing you like**.
bekal: using **харесва ми** and matching it to the number of things
saying you miss something with **липсва ми**

dialogs.title: Диалог — Music and free time
dialogs.intro: Maria and Ani chat after a concert. Notice that in *харесва ми*, the subject is the thing — and the verb agrees with that thing, not with the person.

notes: ⚠️ **Харесва ми flips the sentence around.** Literally it means "it pleases me". The subject is **the thing that is liked**, and you are the receiver. The direct result: **the verb agrees with the number of things, not the number of people.** *Харесва ми филмът* (one thing) but **Харесват** *ми филмите* (several things).

**English actually has a similar pattern, and it can help you.** "I like the film" is straightforward, but "the film **appeals to me**" works exactly like Bulgarian. If you get confused, first think of it as "… appeals to me", then build the sentence.

**Харесва ми and обичам are not the same.** *Обичам* means "love" or "like deeply and lastingly" — used for people, activities, food you always enjoy: *Обичам майка си*, *Обичам да чета*. *Харесва ми* is lighter and often about a particular impression: *Харесва ми този филм* (I like this film).

⚠️ **Харесвам without ми means something else entirely.** *Харесвам те* means "I'm attracted to you" in a romantic sense. If you mean "I like you" as a friend, the pattern is *Харесваш ми* — and even that can still sound like a confession. To be safe: talk about things and activities, not people.

**Липсва ми literally means "it is missing to me" and means "I miss it".** It flips like *харесва ми*, and the verb also agrees with the number of things: *Липсва ми морето* (one), *Липсват ми родителите ми* (several). ⚠️ Don't say *Липсвам Индонезия*; that means "I am missing to Indonesia".
**И на мен ми е трудно uses the long and short forms together** — the pattern you saw in Unit 11. It stresses that the same is true for the speaker. Roughly: "for me too".

**Гайда is the Bulgarian bagpipe**, and it sounds very different from the Scottish one — deeper and heavier. The Rhodope version, **каба гайда**, has a big bag and makes a sound that seems to come from underground.

**Народните песни — Bulgarian folk music is famous for its odd scales and rhythms.** Many songs use seven, eleven or fifteen beats per bar — patterns almost unknown in Western European music. The recordings *Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares* took it around the world in the 1980s, and one Bulgarian song even flew on the Golden Record of the Voyager spacecraft.

grammars.title: Харесва ми — the verb follows the thing
body: Look at the first column: what changes is the verb, following the thing in the third column. The word for the person never changes the verb.
after: The person word uses the short forms you've known since Unit 6: *ми, ти, му, ѝ, ни, ви, им*. It follows the same position rule — it can never be the first word of the sentence.
Other verbs with this flipped pattern: **липсва ми** (I miss), **стига ми** (it's enough for me), **трябва ми** (I need), **става ми** (it fits me), **омръзна ми** (I'm fed up).

grammars.title: … ми е — feelings and states without a subject
body: Neuter adjective + short person word + **е**. This pattern covers almost every statement about feelings and how your body feels.

English
rows: Whatever, it's all the same to me.

after: ⚠️ Compare two sentences that are easy to mix up: **Студено е** means "it's cold (weather)", while **Студено ми е** means "I'm cold". One small word moves the whole meaning from the world to your body.
The past replaces *е* with *беше* or *бе*: *Студено ми беше.* The future: *Ще ми бъде студено.*

blocks.text: To build sentences, combine them with the *да* pattern from Unit 8: *Обичам да готвя.* (I love cooking.) *Не обичам да танцувам.* (I don't like dancing.) *Харесва ми да пътувам.* (I like traveling.)

⚠️ Notice **ходя**, which appears twice. It means "go regularly, usually go", not "be going right now". For something in progress, use *отивам*. *Ходя на кино* = I usually go to the cinema; *Отивам на кино* = I'm on my way to the cinema.

sections.title: Хоро — the dance that will pull you in

blocks.text: Sooner or later you'll be at a Bulgarian party when the music changes, everyone stands up, holds hands or belts, and forms a winding chain. That's the **хоро** (*ho-RO*), and sitting it out is not really an option.

The basic step is simple and repeats; what makes it tricky is the odd rhythm. All you need to do is hold the hand of the person next to you and copy their feet. Nobody notices your mistakes — everyone is busy watching the feet of their own neighbor.

blocks.title: Sentences you'll need that night
items: **Обичам българската музика.** — I love Bulgarian music. This sentence will make everyone in the room turn around.
**Как се казва тази песен?** — What's this song called? Be ready for a long list of recommendations.
**Не мога, но ще опитам!** — I can't, but I'll try! This is the right answer to an invitation to dance, and the only one that will be accepted.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right short person word.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Харесва — Харесват — Харесва — харесват — Харесва — харесва

Много ми харесва. — Липсва ми морето. — Студено ми е. — Трудно ми е. — Обичам да чета.
